content: To effectively manage contact tracing for Ebola Virus Disease (EVD), every identified contact must be interviewed. During the interview, the contact should be asked about their last interaction with the confirmed case. If there is a discrepancy between the date provided by the case and the contact, the most recent date since the case’s symptom onset should be used to start the 21-day follow-up period, which corresponds to the maximum EVD incubation period. When contacts are identified and confirmed, they should be informed of their risk status and the follow-up plan. The Contact Tracing Team should emphasize that early and appropriate clinical care improves outcomes and that immediate isolation reduces the risk of infecting family members. Contacts should also be provided with relevant contact information, such as telephone numbers or hotlines, to report any symptoms. If a contact develops symptoms, they should self-isolate and notify the team immediately to prevent further transmission of EVD. They should also be informed of the importance of notifying the team if they move or leave the area. Any contact found to be symptomatic during the initial interview is considered a potential suspected EVD case. In such cases, the Investigation Team will contact the Field Epidemiologist, who will activate the Case Management Team. The suspected EVD case will then be transported to a transit or isolation unit for further testing. While awaiting EVD testing, contact identification and listing should begin for this new suspected case. The first meeting with a contact is critical for building trust. This meeting should ideally be conducted by an epidemiologist, preferably with psychosocial support present. Trust is essential for ensuring that contacts are truthful about their health status and willing to report symptoms. During this meeting, the Contact Follow-up Team assigned to the contact should be introduced to establish familiarity and rapport. The process of informing the contact of their status should be handled with tact and empathy, avoiding alarming statements such as “Ebola has no treatment” or “Ebola has a very high fatality rate.” Instead, the focus should be on the benefits of being a contact, such as access to immediate medical care if symptoms develop, reduced risk of infecting others, and prompt EVD testing. The Contact Follow-up Team should perform daily visits with the contact at a predetermined location and time. This consistency helps contacts feel comfortable reporting symptoms and allows the team to better understand the contact’s daily activities, ensuring all contacts are consistently monitored. During daily visits, the team will evaluate the contact’s health status through direct observation and by asking questions such as, “How are you feeling?” and “Have you had a fever?” This information should be recorded on the Daily Contact Follow-up Form. Measuring temperature is not required or recommended due to potential risks to contact tracers, but it may be done at the discretion of the country. Symptomatic contacts should never have their temperature taken by the team. After completing the interview or assessment, the team should inquire whether anyone else in the household is unwell, even if they are not a contact. This process, known as “active case finding,” helps identify any sick individuals in the community. If a contact is not at home, the team should attempt to locate them by asking family, neighbors, or community leaders. An explanation for the contact’s absence should be obtained, and the team should report all contacts found and those not found to their assigned Supervisor at the end of each day. The Supervisor should document this information in the Contact Tracing Summary Form and provide it to the Data Manager for analysis. Contacts who complete the 21-day follow-up process without developing symptoms can be discharged. However, no contact can be discharged without being seen and evaluated on or after the 21st day. Discharged contacts may face stigma from their families, peers, or communities. Health communication campaigns and educational activities may be necessary to help reintegrate them into their communities. Community education should emphasize that discharged contacts do not pose a risk of transmitting the disease. Employers may request an official letter declaring the end of follow-up, which should be provided by the EVD response coordinator. To manage cases and their contacts effectively, an electronic database is essential. This database allows for the registration of cases and contacts, the production of daily reports, data export for analysis, geographical mapping of contacts, and visualization of transmission chains. Training for all personnel involved in data collection should be conducted before the first EVD case is identified. Supervisors and Field Epidemiologists should monitor all aspects of the process, including evaluating cases with a low number of reported contacts and ensuring daily visits are conducted. Supervisors should prioritize contacts not reached each day to prevent them from being lost to follow-up. Incentives such as increased wages and health or life insurance may help attract personnel. Training should be provided before employees begin contact tracing, with regular refresher training to reinforce standard operating procedures. It is important to educate Contact Tracing Teams about EVD to alleviate fears and empower them to perform their duties effectively. Maintaining the health and safety of staff is essential. Contact Tracing Teams should avoid direct physical contact with individuals, maintain a distance of at least three feet, and refrain from entering contacts’ homes or sharing meals. Personal protective equipment (PPE) is not needed for Contact Follow-up Teams and should not be worn to avoid alarming communities. Staff should not enter hostile or unwelcoming communities and should contact their Supervisor immediately if problems arise. Scalability is crucial for responding to an increase in cases or contacts. Countries should have plans in place to scale up resources, personnel, and infrastructure as needed. If resources are limited, prioritization of contacts may be considered, although this is not ideal.
